summary: The note is a news story about an unprecedented hailstorm that struck Cairo on a Monday morning, covering the city in white ice. It describes damage to infrastructure, traffic, rural agriculture and the strain on emergency services, along with concerns for ancient monuments. Experts and officials quoted in the piece link the event to wider worries about climate change and call for better preparedness.
one_line: An unprecedented hailstorm hit Cairo, damaging infrastructure, crops and emergency response, and prompting expert warnings about climate change and monument protection.
key_facts: An unlikely hailstorm struck Cairo early on a Monday morning, blanketing much of the city in white.
The hailstorm was caused by a sudden shift in high altitude winds that brought an icy front from the Mediterranean seashore.
Egypt Meteorological Authority described the hailstorm as "extreme and unprecedented".
Palm trees were bent and broken, ancient walkways were covered in ice, and busy streets came to a standstill.
Local shop owner Ahmed Al-Masri said the hailstorm "felt as though the sky were opening up - no one was prepared!"
Rapid hail accumulation collapsed flat roofs in Cairo, causing structural damage to old and new buildings.
Traffic skidded and collided, causing hundreds of minor accidents, and emergency services received thousands of calls at once.
Paramedic Hanaa Mostafa said her ambulances "could barely navigate through icy streets".
Mahmoud Abbas of Cairo Farm, a lifelong date farmer, may lose his whole season's yield because of hail damage to his orchard.
Dr. Lana Fouad of Cairo University's Restoration and Conservation faculty warned that hailstorms can speed up erosion of stone and mortar at the Giza Plateau.
Initial assessments found no major damage to the Great Pyramids and Sphinx, but the storm spurred calls for a review of how to safeguard ancient monuments.
Khaled Nassar of Cairo's Urban Search and Rescue team said, "Cairo is strong; its people are resilient; together we will overcome this."
Dr. Samir Atta of Ain Shams University said individual events cannot definitively be linked to climate change but patterns suggest a departure from normal weather.
Images and videos of the hailstorm went viral on social media, and international aid agencies and foreign governments offered support.
